blogs.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released
blogs.description: PostgreSQL 19 Released Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly t…
blogs.content:
PostgreSQL 19 Released

Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse.

 This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one:

 For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary.

 In practice, that looks like this:

 UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama';
SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn();

 That returns a value like 0/0306EE20 . Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do:

 WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s');
SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama';

 The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time.

 I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia , which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication:

 In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it.

 Here's the relevant MediaWiki code , which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT() .

 Via Lobste.rs

 Tags: mysql , postgresql , replication , scaling , wikipedia , ai-security-research

blogs.content:
Release: llm-gemini 0.38

 Today Google introduced Gemini 4 Neon . I wrote recently about how confusing the pricing for the Gemini 4 series was - Neon has somehow made this even worse.

 Previously the Gemini 4 lineup was Hydrogen, Argon, and Carbon - where Argon and Carbon were the same price , and Hydrogen was 3/4 of that price now but will be 1/4 of that price when the other two double an 1st December once their initial discount pricing expires.

 The Neon announcement pretends that Argon doesn't exist. Here's their new image explaining the model line-up:

 So the lineup now, from most to least expensive, is Carbon, Neon, Hydrogen.

 Except Carbon is currently half price, so right now Neon ($3/million input, $15/million output) is the most expensive of the three - then Carbon ($2/$10), then Hydrogen ($1.50/$7.50). I guess this will make more sense when Carbon doubles to $4/$20 on December 1st.

 I ran some pelicans through the three reasoning levels for Neon - low, medium, high.

 I dropped Argon from my Gemini 4 comparison grid - here's the new Gemini 4 lineup, where the Neon pelicans do look better than Hydrogen and worse than Carbon:

 As I've done with several recent models , I also fired the following prompt against Gemini 4 Neon on "extra" effort level in Google Antigravity:

 Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data

 Here's the result .

 Tags: yonkers-rising , gemini , llm , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , ai , llms , llm-release , google , generative-ai

blogs.content:
Release: datasette-arrows 0.1a0

 Datasette 1.0a43 added the ability for plugins to implement streaming export formats. Datasette core supports streaming CSV and TSV - you can export millions of lines of data from a table without needing to load it all into memory, because those two file formats support streaming data in chunks. The register_output_renderer() plugin hook can now be used to implement the same pattern for other formats.

 I've learned never to release a new plugin feature without accompanying it with a plugin that uses it.

 Claude Fable 5.2 suggested the Apache Arrow streaming format as a good option, and built this plugin in almost a single shot.

 Add the plugin to Datasette ( datasette install datasette-arrows ) and the export dialog gains this new Arrow option:

 This screenshot is from Datasette's main branch - the most recent release doesn't yet group streaming formats such as Arrow with the TSV and CSV in the "All rows in this table" section, but that's coming in the next alpha release.

 Tags: datasette , projects

blogs.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

 Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 12,783 new readers. Google spent most of 2026 being mocked for moving slowly. But something changed this fall, and it’s now shipping faster than ever. Maybe the key is, as Demis Hassabis put it, “alchemy at its finest.”
 The company’s new Neon model is the latest step up both the periodic table and the leaderboard, carrying a mid-tier label but with scores nearing the industry’s best. With one researcher hinting at self-improving AI behind the pace, Google suddenly feels very, very back.

---
 In today’s AI rundown:
 Google’s shipping spree continues with Neon

 Nate’s Notebook: Ask your AI for more

 Use AI to rewrite your LinkedIn profile

 Pika turns AI video into a live film set

 LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

 GOOGLE
 🧪  Google’s shipping spree continues with Neon
 Image source: Google

 The Rundown: Google just released Gemini 4 Neon, a faster sibling to its top-end Carbon that leads Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Sol on most of Google’s tests — marking the company’s fourth Gemini 4 model in under two months.
 The details:
 Despite its mid-tier status, Neon edges Google’s top-end Carbon on Artificial Analysis’ leaderboard at 61, trailing only Claude Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra.

 Google’s testing has Neon beating Opus 5.5 and 6.2 Sol on 16 of 19 benchmarks, with its widest leads in long-document work, office automation, and cyber tasks.

 Neon is now live for Google’s Pro and Ultra tier users, and its API costs $3/$15 per million input/output tokens, a quarter below Opus 5.5 and full-price Carbon.

 The night before launch, Google’s Minkai Xu posted “many people are surprised by how fast RSI moves,” hinting self-improving AI may be behind Google’s pace.

 Why it matters: For most of 2026, Google had every advantage (chips, cash, users) yet was painfully slow to ship frontier options people wanted. Whether it’s recursive self-improvement (RSI) or something else, a switch has flipped internally, and Google’s run through the periodic table (Argon, Carbon, Hydrogen, Neon) is showing up in a big way.

 TOGETHER WITH GOOGLE FOR STARTUPS
 🚀  Startup School: Gemma and Open Models

 The Rundown: Routing every routine prompt through frontier reasoning models destroys startup runways. Google for Startups’ upcoming 4-part live technical series gives you practical blueprints to combine open-weight Gemma models with Gemini across your entire stack.
 What you will gain:
 Run Gemma locally for private, zero-latency inference

 Route high-volume tasks to Gemma; reserve frontier tokens for reasoning

 Fine-tune models using LoRA, QLoRA, and ShieldGemma guardrails

 Benchmark open-source runtimes on Cloud Run and GKE

 Secure your spot .

 NATE’S NOTEBOOK
 🚰  Nate’s Notebook: Ask your AI for more

 The Rundown: Each week, Rundown AI educator Nate Grahek breaks down what he’s seeing while teaching real teams to use AI.
 Nate: Our well pump died at the cabin. The nearest hardware store is 35 minutes away, so one wrong part costs me the afternoon.
 I was on the store’s clunky website, sure this one would stump Claude. I opened the Chrome extension anyway and typed: “Here’s our broken setup. I need water coming out of this faucet, and you can only use parts in stock at this one store.”
 Then I watched it work, page by page. It would pick a pipe, find out it wasn’t in stock, back up, and try another route. It was wandering the aisles for me until it landed on 20 parts from different departments that were all on the shelf.
 I thought that was the whole win. Then I caught myself getting ready to drive over and find all 20 myself. Years of confusing websites have trained me to pick the hassle I know. So I let Claude fill the cart, too. It told me when it was time to enter my credit card, and the whole order was waiting when I got there.
 If you won’t hand a coworker the tedious stuff because it feels rude, this one is for you. I’m that person too, and I brought the same hesitation to AI. I think that feeling holds people back more than their tech skills do.
 Back at the cabin, I almost let it stop me again. My first ask for assembly instructions was fine. Then I pushed for something more ambitious: a step-by-step slide deck. Here are both versions with the prompts I used.
 Try it this week. Install the Claude or ChatGPT browser extension and point it at the site you dread: your health insurance portal, or that old internal tool at work that’s never getting an API.
 Ask for more.

 AI TRAINING
 💼  Use AI to rewrite your LinkedIn profile

 The Rundown: ChatGPT can rewrite your LinkedIn profile for the job you’re moving into, but left to itself, it rounds your story up. In this guide, you’ll have it ask about your real results, write a headline, About section, experience, and skills, then check every claim.
 Step-by-step:
 Copy your LinkedIn headline, About section, one role, and your skills into a note as text, along with two or three job posts you’d apply for

 In ChatGPT, click the Temporary chat at the top right, pick Unpersonalized, and paste a prompt that asks for up to 5 questions first, all at once, and says “Don’t invent numbers, tools, titles, or results,” with your profile and the posts under it

 Answer every question, and say what you haven’t done yet. Then, ask for three headlines under 220 characters and an About section under 2,600 characters

 Next, ask for five experience bullets that start with a verb and up to 10 skills your experience shows

 Ask ChatGPT to check everything it wrote, in a table, and flag anything you didn’t say. Use the corrected versions, and copy them out before you leave the chat

 Pro tip: Before you paste anything into LinkedIn, turn off Share profile updates (Me, then Settings & Privacy, then Visibility) so your network isn’t told about each change.
 Visit The Rundown University to get the full guide, practice resources, and more.

 PRESENTED BY SCRIBE
 🔍 Consultants take months. Scribe takes days.

 The Rundown: Most orgs map workflows the slow way: outside teams, interviews and months of workshops. Scribe Optimize maps how work happens across your org automatically.
 With Scribe Optimize, you can:
 See AI-captured workflow insights in days

 Spot opportunities across teams and tools

 Prioritize improvements based on ROI

 See what’s actually happening in your org .

 AI VIDEO
 🎬 Pika turns AI video into a live film set
 Image source: Pika

 The Rundown: AI video startup Pika just previewed Enact, an experimental tool that works like a live film set, letting users drag actors around, give them spoken notes, and move the camera while the scene keeps playing.
 The details:
 Users can set the stage by grabbing a person or object and moving it mid-scene, with the AI adjusting how it stands and where its shadow falls in the new spot.

 Each actor is a separate AI agent with its own personality that responds to both audio and text direction and can keep track of feedback from earlier takes.

 Once rolling, the camera is controllable throughout the live action, letting users make visual choices just like a director would on set.

 Pika said its team was “startled by how much more real and visceral it feels” to make video this way, though Enact isn’t available to consumers yet.

 Why it matters: A large portion of the world still thinks of AI video as “slop,” but the ramp-up in quality combined with control, speed, and cost-effective models has opened a new outlet for creatives. With real-time video now seeing similar gains, creating an AI video could soon look a lot like what directors are already doing in the real world.

 QUICK HITS

 COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY
 ▸ A reader built a ChatGPT adviser to research contacts
 Today’s workflow comes from an Anonymous Rundown Reader :
 “I often reach out to people I know very little about, whether it's an important email, a text, a potential collaborator, a volunteer request, or prep for a meeting. Researching someone used to take more time than most of these interactions seemed to justify.

Now I use ChatGPT to look into a person's public background, find real common ground, and plan how I'll communicate. The goal isn't to show off what I know about them. It's to communicate more intelligently and naturally.
 I start with a prompt that begins: ‘Act as my personal research, communication, and rapport-building adviser.’ The full prompt also tells the AI to verify identity and important findings, separate facts from interpretation, and avoid inventing a background or assuming someone with a similar name is the right person.
 What I get is a better-informed message, fewer misunderstandings, and a clear record I can return to when the relationship continues.”
 See the workflow on our Community Workflow Hub →

---
 How do you use AI? Tell us for a chance to be featured in the newsletter.

 Microsoft is nearing a ~$500M deal to give TikTok parent ByteDance more access to OpenAI’s models on Azure, a sale that has angered OpenAI over Chinese copycats.

 What we learned
 Protect engineers’ attention

 Evaluate changes to your agents

 Turn recurring failures into self-repair

 What’s next: broader applications, proactive monitoring

 The staggering pace of agentic development has made traditional approaches to performance engineering unsustainable. To keep up, we built the Performance Factory, an autonomous system that uses the full capabilities of Codex and our models to find and fix regressions at an unprecedented speed. The Performance Factory, which runs in the cloud and automates investigating and resolving performance problems, enables us to keep pace with the ambition of our roadmap.

 In the Performance Factory, our engineers define workflows for recurring jobs and write instructions for the Codex agents that carry them out. In particular, the Regression Workflow opens a task when a performance alert fires. An agent investigates the slowdown, records its findings in the task, and proposes a fix for an engineer to review. After deployment, another agent picks up the same task to check whether performance has returned to baseline. From investigating to authoring the fix to verifying mitigation, this first workflow in the Performance Factory has automated the entire process of fixing regressions. In just over three months, the Regression Workflow tracked more than 1,700 investigations and root caused over 600 cases. That’s 17 automated investigations every day.

 Here, we’ll share how our use of Codex evolved into what’s now the Performance Factory, walk through our first running workflow, and share early lessons from building and running agent workflows in production.

 The path from manual investigations to automated workflows

 As we used Codex for more of our performance work, we noticed a progression in how our team worked. We hope other service teams can learn from our process as they adopt agentic workflows in other domains.

 Software work evolves from manual labor to partnering with machines to agent factories.

 1. Pre-Codex . Before Codex, engineers manually examined metrics and logs, compared traces, debugged live machines, and read code to investigate a slowdown. This work was time consuming, and knowing where to look often required deep knowledge of the service. Relevant signals were easy to miss. When we encountered the same kinds of problems repeatedly—like regressions in ChatGPT’s first token latency—we built advanced tools, like CPU and allocation profilers, to make those investigations easier. Over time, we accumulated more than 30 performance tools.

 2. Codex as a partner . Once we had Codex as a partner, engineers could ask, “Why did this get slower?” and work with Codex to investigate, even in an unfamiliar system. Codex could search large codebases, find relevant metrics and traces, follow interactions across services, and do appropriate profiling to piece together what had happened. But engineers still had to steer the process, knowing which performance tools to use and how to guide the investigation. Difficult investigations were more debuggable for more people, with less expertise and time required.

 3. Reusable skills . To automate further, we captured our performance team’s investigation process in a shared skill called perf-forensics . It tells Codex which tools are available, when to use them, and how to work through a slowdown so Codex can try to resolve the problem from a few angles:

 Find when the slowdown began

 Identify the affected requests

 Investigate whether deployments or configuration changes could explain it

 We tested and refined the perf-forensics skill using evals based on past regressions. For the types of regressions we focused on (for example, ChatGPT latency and availability drops), we could now give Codex an alert and get back a diagnosis in a single run, without guiding it through each step.

 4. The human proxy . As we added and refined perf-related Codex skills like perf-forensics , we started to feel like a proxy between our alerts and Codex. An alert would fire, and an engineer would simply copy and paste it into Codex with the right skill, then paste the findings back into Slack.

 5. Automated investigations . Next, we moved investigations to the cloud so an alert could start a Codex session automatically. Codex investigated the slowdown and posted its findings in the Slack thread, but the automation ended with that reply. An engineer still had to pick up the diagnosis, develop a fix, and check whether it worked after deployment. As alerts accumulated, even figuring out which regressions needed attention meant sifting through Slack threads.

 6. The factory . We built the Performance Factory to run end-to-end agentic performance engineering workflows. It tracks what each active task needs next and assigns an agent when that step is ready. Each task keeps its state and findings, so work can pass between agents and engineers and resume after a code review or deployment. For a regression, the work starts with investigating an alert and ends with verifying recovery in production. We can turn common optimizations into workflows that run regularly across our services. A workflow that spots a potential optimization can open a task in another workflow to test and implement it.

 The Performance Factory system’s four parts

 The Performance Factory is made up of four components: a task tracker with configurable workflows, a dispatch loop that assigns ready work to agents, an API that runs Codex in the cloud, and subscriptions that wake agents when something changes (such as a GitHub review comment posting or a deployment completing).

 Performance Factory consists of a task service, dispatch loop, cloud execution, and subscriptions.

 Task service with configurable workflows

 The task service is where engineers define workflows by adding configuration files and prompts for the agents to follow, written in Markdown. The configuration lists the states a task can move through, the allowed transitions, and which steps need an engineer. Separate prompts tell agents what to do at each step.

 Plain text

 1 code-change/

 2 ├── config.toml

 3 └── work/

 4 ├── implementing.md

 5 └── reviewing.md

 A code change task contains a configuration file, along with Markdown prompts for implementing and reviewing.

 Each piece of work becomes a task in a workflow, and all workflows are visible in a UI. Engineers can see what’s open, follow progress, and share a task with a teammate who might have more context or be able to help with the next step.

 Dispatch loop that assigns work

 A dispatch loop periodically checks which tasks are ready for the next step. It assigns an agent to each task by starting a Codex turn with the instructions for the task’s current state. The agent records its progress on the task and moves it to the next state if it completes the step.

 Codex in the cloud

 Once a task is assigned, the agent needs a place to do the work, with access to the same tools an engineer would use. We built an internal API to programmatically invoke a Codex turn in the cloud. The Codex turn runs on an environment inside our network, with access to our code repositories and the observability tools our engineers use, such as metrics, logs, traces, CPU profiles, and memory snapshots.

 The agent runs under a service identity, so we can scope its permissions and see which actions came from our performance agents. Moving agentic work to the cloud lets us run work in parallel without relying on engineers’ laptops being open or manually managing individual cloud development boxes.

 Subscriptions that wake the agent when something changes

 Some work has to wait for a person or a deployment; an agent shouldn’t have to keep running in the meantime. When a task needs to wait, it can subscribe to events like review comments or failed CI checks on a GitHub pull request to get notified when it’s time to pick the work back up. When an incoming event matches the subscription, the task becomes ready again and the dispatch loop can then assign an agent to continue the work.

 The first workflow: from alert to recovery

 Finding, root causing, and solving regressions is the first workflow we built inside the Performance Factory. We call it the Regression Workflow. A performance regression moves through several stages: needs investigation , root caused , fix proposed , and resolved , so we built the automated workflow to reflect and move a task through those same stages.

 When one of its configured performance alerts fires, the Regression Workflow opens a task that agents pick up and move across these stages. The task records its status and key findings outside of any one agent’s context so that other agents or engineers can pick up the work. Engineers can follow the work in Slack or the Regression Workflow UI, add context, and review proposed changes. After a fix is deployed, an agent checks whether the performance has recovered to its original state before resolving the task.

 Performance Factory regression workflow
 A regression is detected. An agent finds the cause and proposes a fix. An engineer takes over and decides what ships. After deployment, the agent wakes up to check recovery. Still regressed? Back to investigation. A regression is detected. A regression is detected.

 Pause

 Z Z

 Detected System
 Find root cause Agent
 Propose fix Agent
 Review & deploy Engineer
 Verify recovery Agent
 Resolved  

 Active stage: Detected

 The Regression Workflow’s steps include finding the root cause, proposing a fix, reviewing and deploying, and verifying recovery.

 Agents find the root cause

 Finding the root cause (or causes) is the first major step in the workflow. The agent starts by figuring out which metrics got worse, when they started to change, and which service requests were affected. The perf-forensics skill gives Codex access to the tools our performance engineers use and a playbook for working through those questions.

 An alert fires when a metric crosses a threshold, but the regression may have started hours earlier. The agent looks back through the data to find when the metric first got worse. It then compares groups of requests: did similar requests actually get slower, or were we serving more requests that were already slow? Those findings point to different causes.

 Once it knows when and where to look, the agent examines deployments and feature flag changes, then reads the relevant code. It checks when a change actually reached the affected requests and uses logs or traces to test whether the code could explain what happened.

 Adversarial review strengthens the diagnosis

 Early on, agents sometimes stopped at the first plausible explanation they found, and some of those diagnoses turned out to be wrong. To catch these mistakes, we added an adversarial review: a separate Codex session...

blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description: An interview with Eric Seufert about agentic commerce, including why he thinks ads will be the answer, and why I want retailers who cater to agents.
blogs.content:
An interview with Eric Seufert about agentic commerce, including why he thinks ads will be the answer, and why I want retailers who cater to agents.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Good morning,

This week’s Stratechery Interview is with longtime Stratechery guest Eric Seufert . Seufert is, in my opinion, the world’s pre-eminent digital advertising analyst, and Stratechery’s most frequent interview subject . Seufert writes full-time at MDM.co , and is well-worth the subscription.

This was one of my favorite interviews I’ve done with Seufert. We see eye-to-eye when it comes to digital advertising, but have some divergences when it comes to agentic commerce. Seufert is adamant that the retailers will make agents that own the experience; my experience argues that consumers will ultimately go to the retailers who welcome agents with open arms.

To that end, in this interview we discuss Seufert’s view — already vindicated! — on agentic shopping, why Amazon is an advertising behemoth across the web, the Meta versus Amazon battle, and how he defines agentic commerce — and where my personal experience disagrees. Then we get into the inevitability of ads in agents, our shared Google optimism, and the current state of OpenAI and Netflix’s ad businesses.

As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

On to the Interview:

An Interview With Eric Seufert About Agentic Commerce

This interview is lightly edited for clarity.

Topics:

Agentic Shopping | The Amazon Identify Layer | Muse | Defining Agentic Commerce | Ad Inevitability | Google | Advertising | ChatGPT and Netflix

Agentic Shopping

Eric Seufert, welcome back to Stratechery. As usual, I’m preparing, I’m like, “How has so much happened in six months? We have so much to talk about” — but before we get there, I went to Mobile Dev Memo to prepare for this interview, MDM.co, is this is a rename?

ES: Yeah, you call it a rename, a rebrand. You know, like Prince going into the symbol, a shorter domain. That’s right.

Shorter domain, also, if you’re talking about advertising, I feel like using an acronym really fits the genre. So there you go.

ES: That’s right, apropos.

We are, I know you’ve been chomping on the bit for this, we are going to talk about agentic shopping. We’ve talked about agentic shopping for a long time. I think you in particular have been very ahead of the curve, you’ve had a very strong opinion on agentic shopping going back a year. We’ve mentioned this article before, Agentic Commerce Is a Mirage . This sort of kicked off this whole series of takes from you. I know we’ve talked about it, but given the context of Muse, of Instinct, all these things that are happening, and the fact that we’re going to spend a long time on the topic, why don’t you start from the top? This is your chance to sort of restate your case, and then we’re going to jump ahead to some of the stuff you’ve written more recently.

ES: Yeah, so let me set the stage on the original article, I published that September 2025. And the context of that piece was not Muse, it was not Instant Checkout, those came later, this was Amazon blocking Perplexity.

Now, remember, Perplexity launched probably the OG agent. I’m sure it wasn’t the first, but maybe it was the first that got any sort of attention. And I said, “Of course they did”, why wouldn’t they? Doesn’t that serve their interests? First of all, Amazon has historically had a pretty hostile relationship with third-party browsing agents and it just kind of made sense.

Right, which has always been like an eternal battle for them. Those things that stick in a coupon code or look for a comparison site, all those sorts of things.

ES: Yeah. And so I made the case that, of course, they would block Perplexity and of course, they would want to protect their first-party relationship with consumers, because that is the source of a lot of the commercial value that is generated by the company, because a lot of the net income is generated from advertising. So if they got disintermediated by an agent, then no one would see their ads and they would lose that source of high-margin revenue, which would be disastrous for the business.

By the way, that revenue funds a lot of other parts of the business that are really good for consumers and so if consumers lost access to those parts of the business, then they’d be worse off.

If it all went away they would have to raise prices, which would decrease volume, which would actually just make everyone unhappy.

ES: Yeah, exactly. In the agentic commerce outcome that some people are championing for — but I think also that the tenor of this has changed a lot in the last few months.

Yep, so let’s fast forward. You accurately predicted this in this context — to your credit, you had written this before ChatGPT’s commerce initiative came out, you immediately said it was going to fail. Fast forward a year, is Muse and Instinct more of the same? Give me the path from the Perplexity story to where we are today.

ES: (laughing) Well, so the series is on part five after a year, so there have been a number of twists and turns in the last 13 months. But what you see is Amazon very stridently digging its heels in and saying, “We will not open our platform to third-party agents, that does not serve our interests”.

There was one point — in February, Jassy had made this comment at Davos saying, “We might find a way to work with third-party agents, but it would have to make sense for us, and there’d have to be a value exchange”, and he made a similar comment in the Q1 earnings, or maybe the Q4 earnings, shortly thereafter.

But I wrote another one of the entries from the series in response to those comments and I said, “The way to do that is with ads, the value exchange is with ads”. This was actually around the same time that there were rumors that Amazon was going to invest in OpenAI, and I said, look, maybe they do invest in OpenAI — they hadn’t committed to that yet — but if they do, I bet the reason will not be because they want to orchestrate some sort of agentic commerce exchange where people can search Amazon through ChatGPT, I bet it’s so that they can insert ads into ChatGPT. And that got announced just recently , and that, I think, is really meaningful and really telling.

I think there are two clues as to what form this will ultimately resolve to. One of them is this ads deal that hasn’t really taken shape yet, but we can kind of hypothesize as to what that might look like, it might just be Amazon inserting ads via its DSP into ChatGPT. But that is win-win — that’s win-win-win, actually. The consumer wins, ChatGPT wins, and Amazon wins. Amazon wins because it gets more surface area to broadcast its advertisers’ ads to.

And as we’ve talked about, there is no bigger bullish signal for an advertising platform than increased inventory. You actually want the price-per-ad to be going down, because there’s so many more places to put it, that’s how the marketplace dynamics work for these ads, so that is a great outcome for Amazon.

ES: It’s a great outcome for Amazon, because they’re inventory-constrained, they’re not data-constrained, they’ve got more data than anybody else — they’re inventory-constrained and they don’t have a social surface. They’ve infamously failed to generate real traction with any sort of social product outside of maybe Twitch, and the advertising product there has not really gained too much steam.

So everyone wins, ChatGPT wins because they get more demand, so the price is going to go up. Amazon wins because they get to broadcast their advertisers’ ads elsewhere using their data, which means they’ll be very well targeted, because I would assume there’s going to be some sort of account linking — but even if there isn’t, they still get identity, we can talk about that in a second.

And the consumer wins. Why? Previously they got no access to Amazon products in their ChatGPT conversations, now they do. Now they can discover Amazon products. And guess what? They get to discover the most relevant product. Why? Because it was priced, and it was bid against, and it was served by Amazon. That’s win, win, win.

The Amazon Identify Layer

By the way, a couple questions on this, just in passing — we’re going to continue on this thread. Whatever happened to the Amazon-Meta partnership, where you were going to be able to sign into Amazon on Meta platforms and there would be ads coming straight from Amazon? Did that just peter out completely?

ES: I think so, that was always a test, they did the same thing with Snap. That was the genesis of my Walled Compound idea. But the idea persists, I don’t think it went anywhere with Meta, and it didn’t go anywhere.

Maybe it just makes more sense because OpenAI is a nascent ad business, so Amazon can provide them a lot more value, whereas the hurdle rate for Meta to allow someone else to advertise on the platform is extraordinarily high.

ES: Yeah, it’s just really high, and also keep in mind, in that partnership Amazon was going to select the ad, so Meta was effectively giving up control over what appeared in the feed. But I think what’s interesting about that idea is that it does persist.

The thing about Amazon that you have to recognize, especially in the context of agentic commerce, but even more broadly, is that Amazon is the identity layer for the Internet . It is the identity backbone for the entirety of the open Internet. That is the open Internet, it’s Amazon, it’s Amazon’s bid, it’s Amazon identity.

Really? Explain this. Why is it Amazon and not Google or Facebook, which people would assume?

ES: Because they are walled gardens. Amazon has deterministic identity on 90% of US households. And so when you see a deal that Amazon does with Roku, with Disney+, with Netflix, with Tubi, with OpenAI, with Pinterest, the reason that those other parties are willing to allow somebody to inject demand into their bid stream, into their ecosystem, is because Amazon has the identity, they know who they are. And so when Amazon can connect that person to their data set from Amazon Prime, they’re going to target ads better than almost anyone else could.

Wasn’t this formerly Google’s domain? Are you saying they’re taking over what Google Networks used to be?

ES: Google Networks still exist, but they weren’t doing the targeting — they were effectively allowing the ads to be served, the ads would be served against cookies. But what Amazon is doing is different, because Amazon says we don’t need a cookie.

Because you’re signing into the Amazon account and linking it to that other service?

ES: You might be. In some cases, you are. In some cases, you aren’t. Amazon says we don’t need cookies, we don’t need device IDs in order to do that identity, we just have all these other signals that we can place the user against.

Fascinating.

Muse

Let’s go back to the question with agents. The angle from Amazon is super clear, especially the serving ads angle — they want to own the user, they want to own the relationship, they collect all the data. The angle for OpenAI makes a ton of sense, they’re building an ad business, and if Amazon can inject basically tons of money into their business by offering way better ads than they ever could, that makes total sense. But then we run into Muse. When I asked about what happened to that partnership, could it be resuscitated in this case? Right now it looks like they’re just in a face-off. What’s your take on what’s happening there?

ES: Here’s my take. I think that Meta internally recognizes that Muse will be monetized with ads at some point. I think if they came straight out of the gate and said, “Hey, we’ve got this totally new consumer paradigm, it’s called an agent, it does work on your behalf, and by the way, you’re going to give it a lot of infor...

blogs.title: Apple Permissions Update, The New App Paradigm, My iPhone Duo Review
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description: Apple doesn't ruin the Mac, but they don't fix the agent problem, raising questions if they can think outside the app paradigm. Then, my iPhone Duo review.
blogs.content:
Apple doesn't ruin the Mac, but they don't fix the agent problem, raising questions if they can think outside the app paradigm. Then, my iPhone Duo review.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Good morning,

On last week’s Sharp Tech , Andrew and I discussed Jensen Huang’s resignation and what that meant for Nvidia, as well as why I think the China chip ban is a bad idea. We also discuss Andrew’s Sharp Text article, Jensen Huang Was Always Going to Lose , about his misadventures in Washington D.C. Plus, as a palate cleanser, I recount my early adventures in 3D-printing.

Then, on Sunday’s subscriber-only mailbag , we discuss Intel and AMD’s criss-crossing fortunes, whether the frontier is shrinking, and why the hyperscalers are well-positioned.

On to the Update:

Apple Permissions Update

From 9to5Mac :

Last month, Apple announced its plans to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access amid the rise of “increasingly capable and autonomous” AI agents. With today’s new macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is implementing several changes as part of this…

In macOS 27.2, “Device Control and Data Access” is a unified toggle in System Settings, where Apple says that apps with that level of access can “view and send email, edit contacts and photos, monitor your keyboard, track websites, record your screen, control any app on your Mac, and more.” In macOS 27.3, Apple is splitting “Device Control and Data Access” into two categories:

Accessibility: Intended specifically for assistive technologies, with permissions handled through an entitlement process.

System and App Protection Override: A new category for apps that need to bypass certain macOS protections to control other apps or perform automated tasks.

For the latter, users will be able to specify which apps an automation tool can access rather than granting it unrestricted control. For instance, you could give an app access to the Mail app, but not Messages. macOS 27.3 also adds an option for users to require an app to request permission every time it needs access, rather than granting it access indefinitely…

Crucially, Apple isn’t removing the ability to give an app Full Disk Access. If you deem it necessary, you can still give an app Full Disk Access. However, Apple is redesigning the approval process to make the implications of that decision more obvious.

I wrote about Apple’s Full Disk Access warning in October with some trepidation:

To say that I’m nervous about what Apple’s solution will entail is a massive understatement. There is one aspect in which the Mac is the perfect agent host: Apple has, for decades, invested in a combination of scriptability, automation, and accessibility APIs (these are very often the same thing) that makes it remarkably well-suited to computer use. Then there is the fact that macOS is a certified Unix system; this means that agents — which are perfectly suited to the command line — have access to the entire universe of tooling built for Unix systems. And, of course, Mac hardware is amazing.

The problem is that for my particular use case — a headless, always-on Mac Mini that I primarily access from other computers and my phone through the ChatGPT and Claude apps — macOS is incredibly hostile. The biggest issue is GUI-only permission prompts that are invisible to software running on said computer, including agents.

I’m not going to dive back into the details of why those permission prompts are so maddening, but for what it’s worth, this announcement did not make things worse; it also did not really fix the problem, and I think it’s pretty interesting to consider why that is. Yes, this is a personal hobbyhorse of mine, but there is a broader point to be made.

The New App Paradigm

Go back to September’s iPhone event, and my critique of CEO John Ternus’ framing of the iPhone as “the intelligent personal hub”:

It’s extremely impressive that Apple claims 300,000 apps work with Siri. Note, however, that the implication of it being “easy for developers to adopt new capabilities” is that developers have to actually put in the work — that’s work in addition to updating their UI for Duo. In a world where everyone has to convince developers to build integrations, this wouldn’t be an issue. However, this is where browser use looms large: to the extent that agents can just use the web is the extent to which they get an integration with basically everything for free, and it’s Apple, with its dependency on developers plugging into APIs, who is at a disadvantage…

This is a subtler point, but perhaps the most profound: in Apple’s vision, the utility of Intelligence is defined by its ability to augment your existing workflow. Thus the reference to updating your calendar and reminders. It’s very possible, however, that the better workflow is to outsource a lot of work that used to happen in apps to the agent directly. What’s better, using a structured reminders app that you have to check, or simply being reminded directly by an agent? In truth the answer will likely vary by person, but it’s worth pointing out that Apple is so married to the app paradigm that they probably never even considered the alternative.

This is actually exactly what happened with this update. First, full disk access still exists, just with much scarier warnings, and I’m fine with that: it’s good for users to know what they are getting into. Second, there is some genuine loosening of permissions with the new “System & App Protection Override”: as I understand it, this gives specific applications broad-based permissions to do things like control other apps, and I assume (hope) all of the other capabilities that it might need, and you only need to ask once. This is helpful!

At this point, however, I’ve granted ChatGPT and Claude all of the permissions they might ever want or need, and I still deal with permissions dialogs, and it’s for a vector that doesn’t seem to be on Apple’s radar. Specifically, Apple is very concerned with apps controlling other apps; my use case, however, is two apps — ChatGPT and Claude — making other apps.

These apps are barely apps: I have a whole fleet of little apps that manage the channels listings for various sports leagues; these apps need to access the tuner devices on my network, which means they need to be able to see devices on the local network — that means a GUI-only permission dialog (although while proof-reading, ChatGPT may have found a fix for this specific permission ).. Another example is that I bought a networked label printer: instead of using the (terrible) Mac app, Claude built an app that controls it directly; that needed a permissions dialog. Indeed, I basically do not use any new software anymore: if I need something, I custom build it on the spot — but then I hit permissions dialogs!

(As a side note, I do have an ethernet KVM attached to my Mac Mini, which allows my agents to view the screen from outside the OS; this let the agents tell me that a permissions request was on the screen, but they would refuse to click “OK”. In this Fable 5.2 is a wonderful surprise: I’ve made clear to the agents that the Mac Mini they run on is their Mac Mini — I don’t have any personal information on there — and Fable now cites that and willingly clicks “OK”. I feel silly at how happy this makes me.)

Unfortunately, Apple’s changes don’t address this issue at all, at least as far as I can tell. To go back to my September critique, Apple is very focused on a world of apps, and to the extent they are thinking about agents, they are thinking about agents controlling apps that already exist. The future, however, isn’t about apps at all, at least not as we presently think about them: it’s about making new ones, on demand, for specific use cases; the fact I have to give all of these one-offs special permissions really does drive me crazy. More pertinently to this Update, it continues to raise questions in my mind as to whether Apple is even capable of imagining a future where capital-A Apps are things to avoid, not reasons to buy.

---

My iPhone Duo Review

Meanwhile, to go back to that iPhone event, I sadly cracked the screen on my beloved iPhone Air, and was in the market for a new phone sooner than I expected; thanks to Daman — whose voice you hear reading quotes on the podcast recordings of these Updates — I managed to snag a walk-in iPhone Duo. I was certain it wasn’t for me, but I figured it would be worth it just for the content.

It turns out I love it — and, interestingly enough, what I love appears to be a late realization for Apple. Again from 9to5Mac :

In today’s iOS 27.3 beta release, Apple is introducing two changes for iPhone Duo users. Most notably, it adds a new face recognition option that lets you unlock your iPhone Duo by looking at it. Apple is also adding an option to have your iPhone Duo lock when you close it.

The facial recognition — don’t call it Face ID, which projects 30,000 infrared dots on your face to make a 3D depth map — is getting the headlines, but it’s the second feature that stands out to me. When Apple announced the Duo they included this incredible animation:

This iPhone duo animation https://t.co/y7NftWpyXS

— Marques Brownlee (@MKBHD) September 9, 2026

The implication is clear: you can use your iPhone on the small screen, seamlessly transition to the big screen, and go back again. It’s also totally unrealistic, at least that last part.

Here’s my take on the iPhone Duo: to me it’s a big iPhone Air. What I love about the Air — and after using the Air, hated about the iPhone Pro — is the feel of it in my hand. It’s so thin and light that it’s genuinely a pleasure to hold, and the big screen of the Duo is amazing to use. Apple really nailed the big screen UI, particularly multi-tasking.

Now obviously, I can’t fit an unfolded Duo in my pocket, thus the fold. But that is purely a matter of logistics: I would never willingly go from the big screen to the small screen while using the phone ; why would I want to so severely compromise my experience when I already went to the trouble of opening the screen (or, when I’m at home, basically never closing it)? To that end, requiring a separate action to lock the phone after folding it up was bizarre. I found myself forgetting to lock the phone all of the time, and the fact that is the default suggests that Apple was actually captured by their animation, and not how people might actually use this thing. Now it’s much clearer: when you need to go you close the phone and you put it in your pocket, and that’s that.

Now, when you’re out and about and need to look at a message, having something akin to Face ID is definitely a big improvement; Apple clearly should have put Face ID on the outside of the phone, even if it was impossible to add on the inside. That’s fine! They are not two sizes of the same phone; they are two completely distinct experiences that happen to be in the same physical device.

More generally, John Gruber made a great point on this morning’s Dithering that what is exciting about Apple’s current iPhone lineup is that it is compromised. You have the base iPhone, which is fine, but then the iPhone Pro goes all out for power and performance and battery life, at the cost of size and weight; the Air goes all out for size and weight, at the cost of battery life and the camera; the Duo goes all out for that incredible big screen, at the cost a compromised portable experie...
